paragraphs: One who delays relieving himself transgresses the prohibition of "you shall not make yourselves detestable," whether regarding solid or liquid waste; but with liquid waste there is an additional concern of danger, and even of sterility, if this becomes habitual through delay. There are people who stumble in this: when the urge comes upon them while they are studying or occupied with their affairs, they do not get up promptly, thinking, "I will finish this a little more," or "until I finish this page of the Zohar or this psalm" - and this is a great folly, for this is "a mitzvah performed through a transgression." One must therefore be very careful about this. And the Chesed LeAlafim wrote in the name of the Kabbalists that one who is lenient in this matter deprives himself of purity of thought. One who cares for his soul and wishes to cleave to his Maker must be careful that his body be clean at all times; this also benefits the health of the body and makes him, as it were, a new creature.

clarification.explanation: One who delays relieving himself transgresses the prohibition of "you shall not make yourselves detestable," both regarding solid and liquid waste - except that with liquid waste (urination) there is an additional concern of danger and even of sterility, in that a person can become sterile if he habitually delays. Some people stumble in this: when they feel the need while studying or occupied with something else, they do not get up right away but think "I'll finish this in a little while" or "until I finish this page of the Zohar or this psalm" - and this is a great error, for this is "a mitzvah performed through a transgression" (a mitzvah accomplished by way of a sin). One must therefore be very careful about this. The Chesed LeAlafim writes in the name of the Kabbalists that one who is lenient about this harms the purity of his thought. One who wishes to cleave to his Maker must make sure that his body is clean at all times - this also benefits bodily health, and causes a person to become, as it were, a "new creature."
takeaways: Delaying relief (whether solid or liquid waste) transgresses "you shall not make yourselves detestable," and with liquid waste there is also a concern of danger and sterility.

One must not put off relieving oneself with the excuse "I'll finish in a little while" - this is a mitzvah performed through a transgression, and one must keep the body clean at all times for the sake of purity of thought.

paragraphs: Also when lying in bed at night, if he feels the need to relieve himself, he should gather himself to get up, and not be lazy or negligent because of cold, rain, darkness, or the like. But he must first wash his hands properly, for he cannot walk four cubits and rub or wipe himself while an evil spirit still rests upon his hands. However, since he now needs to relieve himself, he cannot recite the blessing "al netilat yadayim" [on the washing of the hands] yet - rather he should relieve himself first, and afterward recite "al netilat yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar." He must therefore be careful not to interrupt with speech from the time he washes his hands until he enters the bathroom and washes a second time and recites the blessing. See the Shulchan Aruch of Rabbeinu Zalman, siman 6, se'if 3.

clarification.explanation: Even when a person is lying in bed at night, if he feels the need to relieve himself, he should gather himself and get up promptly - not being lazy because of cold, rain, darkness, and the like. But before going, he must first wash his hands properly, for one cannot walk four cubits while an "evil spirit" rests upon unwashed hands. Since at this moment he already needs to relieve himself, he cannot recite the blessing "al netilat yadayim" right away - rather he should first relieve himself, and only then recite "al netilat yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar" together. He must therefore be careful not to interrupt with speech from the first washing until he enters the bathroom, washes again, and recites the blessing.
takeaways: When getting up at night out of need, one should wash hands first (without a blessing), relieve oneself, then wash again and recite "al netilat yadayim" and "Asher Yatzar" together - without interrupting with speech throughout.

paragraphs: Anyone who can hold himself for the duration of walking a parsah does not transgress "you shall not make yourselves detestable," nor is there any concern of danger, whether regarding solid or liquid waste. Some say that even one who cannot hold himself for that duration - if the expelling force is not able to overpower the retaining force except with a bit of assistance, by the person pressing himself slightly to expel the waste - this is not called "delaying relief" deliberately so as to transgress "you shall not make yourselves detestable," since the expelling force needs his own slight assistance of pressing; and his not pressing is merely "sitting and doing nothing." But if his urge becomes so strong that the expelling force overpowers the retaining force to expel the waste without any need for the assistance of pressing, even slightly, then he does transgress "you shall not make yourselves detestable" if he delays relieving himself - as the Gaon Rabbeinu Zalman writes on this in the Shulchan Aruch, siman 3, se'if 11.

clarification.explanation: Anyone who can hold himself back (delay the need) for the time it takes to walk a parsah (four mil) does not transgress "you shall not make yourselves detestable," and there is no concern of danger, neither with solid nor liquid waste. Some hold that even if he cannot hold himself for so long, as long as the expelling force (the urge to go) is not stronger than the retaining force, but rather only with a bit of effort on his part (light pressing) can he expel the waste - this is not considered deliberate delay transgressing "you shall not make yourselves detestable," because the expelling force itself needs his slight assistance, and as long as he does not press, he is merely "sitting and doing nothing" (a passive state). But if the urge intensifies to the point that the expelling force completely overpowers the retaining force, so that the waste could come out without any need for assistance at all - delaying in such a state transgresses "you shall not make yourselves detestable."
takeaways: One who can delay the need for a long time (the duration of walking a parsah), or who needs slight assistance (pressing) to expel, does not transgress by delaying.
Only when the expelling force overpowers entirely on its own, without need of assistance, does delaying in that state transgress "you shall not make yourselves detestable."

paragraphs: One should be careful to close the door of the bathroom even at night in darkness, for the sake of modesty, for the Semak and other early authorities counted modesty among the mitzvot of the Torah. And even though there are those who disagree and hold that this is rather an admonition of our Sages, a good trait for which Israel was praised, nevertheless one must be even more careful about it, since there are those who hold it is from the Torah. Nonetheless, if there is a bad smell in the bathroom that is very hard on him, and he opens the door to let in some air, one may be lenient about this in the darkness of night when no one sees him. And know that the admonition of modesty in the bathroom is not fundamentally about the exposure itself, for we do not find that they were strict about exposing the whole body when going to immerse or in the bathhouse and the like. Rather, the reason here is built upon the introduction I wrote above in the name of Rabbeinu the Ari, in Sha'ar Ma'amrei Rashbi, Parashat Tetzaveh, concerning the point of the "back" mentioned above; and see also what I wrote in the name of Rabbeinu [the Ari] in Sha'ar HaMitzvot, Parashat Shemini, mentioned above. Understand from this that the mice commonly found in the bathroom are analogous to the kelipot [husks/shells of impurity], and from this you will understand the reason they were strict about modesty in the bathroom - that thereby the evil spirits are subdued.

clarification.explanation: One must be careful to close the door of the bathroom even at night in complete darkness, for reasons of modesty - since several of the early authorities (such as the Semak) counted modesty among the mitzvot of the Torah itself. Although there are those who disagree and hold that this is only a rabbinic enactment (a good trait for which Israel was praised), one should nevertheless be even more careful about it, since some hold it to be a Torah obligation. Still, if there is a bad smell in the bathroom, and the person there needs to open the door a bit to get some relief, it is permitted to be lenient about this on a dark night when no one can see him. The Ben Ish Chai explains that the main reason for modesty in the bathroom is not related to the exposure of the body itself (since we do not find such strictness regarding immersion or the bathhouse), but is based on the secret mentioned above: that this place is a place where the kelipot draw their nourishment (similar to the mice commonly found in bathrooms, which are an analogy to the kelipot), and therefore they were strict about modesty there, in order to subdue the evil spirits that rest there.
takeaways: One should close the bathroom door even in darkness, for reasons of modesty - which has both an important halachic aspect and an aspect of secret (subduing the forces of impurity that rest there).
In the case of a strong bad smell, it is permitted to be lenient and open the door slightly at night when no one can see.

paragraphs: One should not expose himself until he sits, and it is proper not to expose more than two handbreadths in front and one handbreadth behind. But if the place is soiled and there is a concern that his clothes will become soiled, he need not be careful about this, but should expose as much as necessary according to the place; and whatever can be minimized in exposure should be minimized, as the Rav Chesed LeAlafim wrote. Likewise, wherever there is concern of soiling, one may be lenient in a bathroom that has partitions and a closed door. Therefore, in our time, when most bathrooms have partitions and a closed door, one need not be so strict about the matter of exposure.

clarification.explanation: One should not expose the body until seated, and it is proper not to expose more than two handbreadths in front and one handbreadth in back. But if the place is soiled and there is concern that clothing will become dirty, one need not be careful about this, but should expose only as much as is necessary given the place - and wherever possible to minimize exposure, one should minimize it. Likewise, in any place where there is concern of soiling (such as a bathroom with partitions and a closed door), one may be lenient regarding exposure, and therefore nowadays, when most bathrooms are surrounded by partitions and a closed door, one need not be so strict about this matter.
takeaways: One should avoid unnecessary exposure of the body in the bathroom (up to two handbreadths in front and one handbreadth behind), but in modern bathrooms with partitions and doors, this stringency is relaxed.

paragraphs: Two people should not go together to the bathroom - and not only two men, but even two women should not enter together; rather each one should enter alone and close the door behind him. And the Chesed LeAlafim wrote that one should caution about this even regarding young children, whether so that they become accustomed to modest conduct, or so that they do not become accustomed to licentious conduct - even with young children who do not yet know how to do evil, for the Gemara says that a woman should not stand to urinate in front of a nursing infant, and how much more so with older children.

clarification.explanation: Two people should not enter the bathroom together - not only two men, but even two women should not enter together; rather each one should enter alone and close the door. The Chesed LeAlafim writes that one must be careful about this even with young children - both so that they become accustomed to modest conduct, and so that they do not become accustomed to licentious conduct, even if they are young and do not yet know how to distinguish good from evil - for the Gemara says that a woman should not urinate in front of a nursing infant, and all the more so with older children.
takeaways: One should not enter the bathroom in pairs, even people of the same gender, and even with young children - in order to instill modesty and prevent licentiousness.

paragraphs: When relieving himself in an open field, he should distance himself so that his fellow cannot see his exposure, what he uncovers of his flesh in front and behind. He need not distance himself so far that his fellow cannot see him at all - only so that his fellow will not see his exposed parts - but he may relieve himself behind a fence even if close enough that his fellow can hear the sound of his "lower sneeze," for hearing the sound of a "lower sneeze" is not forbidden on account of modesty, but is rather a matter of shame and embarrassment for most people, and one who is not particular about it is not particular. And indeed, in the days of the Sages of the Talmud they were not particular about this, as the Gaon Rabbeinu Zalman writes in the Shulchan Aruch.

clarification.explanation: One who relieves himself in an open field must distance himself so that his fellow cannot see what he exposes of his body in front and behind. He need not distance himself so far that his fellow cannot see him at all, but only so that his fellow will not see his exposed parts - but it is permitted to relieve oneself behind a fence even if close enough for his fellow to hear the sound (the sound that is heard). Hearing such a sound is not a prohibition of modesty but only a matter of common shame and embarrassment, and one who is not particular about it is not particular; indeed, in the days of the Sages of the Talmud they were not particular about this.
takeaways: In an open field one must distance oneself so that no one sees the exposed body, but there is no need to distance oneself so that no sound at all is heard - that is a matter of personal embarrassment, not a prohibition of modesty.

paragraphs: And all this modesty was stated only regarding solid waste, but urination was permitted even in front of many people and in daytime, because of the concern of danger, lest it become habitual [to become sterile]. Therefore it is forbidden to practice modesty and wait if one needs to do so; nevertheless, one should step aside somewhat - and even a woman [should step aside] from her young son. See the Shulchan Aruch of Rabbeinu Zalman.

clarification.explanation: All the laws of modesty mentioned were stated only regarding solid waste, but urination was permitted even in front of many people and in the daytime, out of concern for danger (sterility) - and therefore it is forbidden to practice modesty and delay if there is a need. Nevertheless, it is proper to step aside somewhat to the side - even if it is a woman with her young son.
takeaways: Urination is permitted even in front of many people, and one should not delay for the sake of modesty due to concern of danger - but it is proper to step aside somewhat.

paragraphs: In a place not surrounded by partitions, it is forbidden to relieve oneself of solid waste facing east-to-west; rather one should relieve oneself facing north-to-south. But in a place with partitions, it is permitted even so, even in a large courtyard, and even if there is only a single partition to the west - one sits next to the partition, close to it, and relieves himself with his back to the west, toward the partition; and if it is to the east, he sits beside it with his back to the east. The measure of this partition need not be ten handbreadths high - rather, anything that prevents his exposure from being seen is sufficient; therefore if it is small, he should relieve himself right beside it, in a manner that it shields him so his exposure is not revealed. And some say that even in a place with partitions, one should be precise about this, not relieving oneself east-to-west but only north-to-south, and it is proper to be concerned for their words. And here in our city of Baghdad, may it be guarded, the widespread custom is not to build a bathroom in a house or courtyard that has partitions except in a manner that one relieves oneself facing north-to-south.

clarification.explanation: In a place without partitions, it is forbidden to perform solid-waste relief while facing between east and west; rather one should face between north and south. But in a place with partitions, it is permitted in any direction, even in a large courtyard - and even if there is only one partition (for example, to the west), the person sits close to it with his back toward the western partition (or the eastern one, if that is where it is). The measure of the partition need not be ten handbreadths high - anything that prevents exposure of the body is sufficient; therefore if the partition is small, one should sit right beside it so that it shields the body from being exposed. Some hold that even in a place with partitions, one should be careful not to perform solid-waste relief facing east-to-west but only north-to-south, and it is proper to be concerned for their view. In Baghdad the accepted custom was not to build a bathroom in a house or courtyard facing east-west, but only in a direction allowing relief facing north-to-south.
takeaways: Without partitions it is forbidden to perform solid-waste relief facing east-west, only north-south; with partitions it is permitted in any direction, though it is proper to be stringent and prefer north-south there as well.

paragraphs: One should not speak any words in the bathroom, even mundane words, even a single word, for the external forces [of impurity] attach themselves to the letters of the speech he speaks there. But it is permitted to snore, since this does not produce letters from his mouth.

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to speak any words at all in the bathroom, even mundane words, even a single word, because the forces of impurity (the "external ones") attach themselves to the letters of speech that come out there from a person's mouth. However, it is permitted to snore (to make a sound through the nose), since this is not considered producing letters from the mouth.
takeaways: One must not speak at all in the bathroom, even a single word, because the forces of impurity attach themselves to the letters of speech - but snoring is permitted since it does not produce letters.

paragraphs: One should be careful to wipe well, for feces at the anus delays prayer, and the essential cleaning is with water, as it is written, "and is not washed of his filthiness" (Proverbs 30:12). And the custom in the lands of Edom to wipe with paper or a cloth is not clean enough for this.

clarification.explanation: One must be careful to wipe well after relieving oneself, for remnants of feces at the anus delay prayer (prevent one from praying). The essential cleaning must be with water, as it is written, "and is not washed of his filthiness" (a hint to the obligation of washing). The widespread custom in the lands of Europe (called "the cities of Edom") to wipe only with paper or a cloth is not sufficient for proper cleanliness.
takeaways: One should wash with water after relieving oneself, and not rely only on wiping with paper or a cloth, since remaining feces delays prayer.

paragraphs: If one urinated or relieved himself and forgot to recite the blessing, if more than half an hour has passed, he should not recite "Asher Yatzar" with God's name and sovereignty [invoked]; but within half an hour, he should recite it. And if he is in doubt whether he recited it or not, he should not recite it with God's name and sovereignty, but should contemplate the name and sovereignty in his heart. And if he urinated or relieved himself twice in succession, he should recite the blessing only once.

clarification.explanation: One who urinated or relieved himself and forgot to recite "Asher Yatzar": if more than half an hour has passed, he should no longer recite the full blessing with God's name and sovereignty; but if it is still within half an hour, he may recite the full blessing. If he is unsure whether he already recited it or not, he should not recite it with the full formula, but should only contemplate the blessing in his heart. If he relieved himself twice in succession, he does not recite the blessing twice, but only once.
takeaways: A forgotten "Asher Yatzar" blessing may be made up within half an hour; beyond that, or in case of doubt, one should not recite the full blessing but only contemplate it silently.
Relieving oneself twice in succession requires only a single blessing.

paragraphs: One who ate something requiring a concluding blessing, and before he recited it he urinated or relieved himself, should recite "Asher Yatzar" first, and afterward the concluding blessing, since the blessing "Asher Yatzar" is recited more frequently.

clarification.explanation: One who ate a food that requires a concluding blessing, and before reciting it needed to urinate or relieve himself, should recite "Asher Yatzar" first, and only afterward the concluding blessing on the food - since the blessing "Asher Yatzar" is recited more frequently (and therefore takes precedence).
takeaways: When there is a conflict between a concluding blessing on food and the blessing "Asher Yatzar," one should recite "Asher Yatzar" first, since it is recited more frequently.

paragraphs: Although it is permitted to kill a louse with the fingers of the right hand, and it is likewise permitted to rub off drops of urine with them, nevertheless it is forbidden to wipe [oneself] with the fingers of the right hand, because one binds the tefillin with them; rather one should wipe with the fingers of the left hand, for there one does not wind the tefillin around the fingers but around the arm. He must therefore be careful not to wipe with the finger around which the three windings are made, called the "amah" [the finger designated for this purpose], but should set that finger aside and wipe with the other two fingers. And if this is not possible for him due to excessive filth, such that he cannot clean himself well with only two fingers, then he should wipe with all his fingers, including that one. And women too, who have no tefillin, should accustom themselves to wipe with the left hand and not the right, for there are additional reasons for this that apply to them as well.

clarification.explanation: Although it is permitted to kill a louse with the fingers of the right hand, and likewise permitted to rub off drops of urine with them, nevertheless it is forbidden to wipe oneself with the fingers of the right hand, since the tefillin straps are bound with these fingers. One should therefore wipe with the fingers of the left hand, since most of the winding of the tefillin there is around the arm (aside from the final three windings on the finger called the "amah," as detailed below). One must be especially careful not to wipe with the finger on which the three windings are made (called the "amah"), but should skip it and wipe with the other two fingers. If, due to excessive filth, it is not possible to manage with only two fingers, then one should wipe with that finger as well. Women too, who have no tefillin, should accustom themselves to wipe with the left hand rather than the right, since there are additional reasons for this that apply to them as well.
takeaways: One should wipe after relieving oneself with the fingers of the left hand rather than the right (since the fingers of the right hand bind the tefillin), and should especially avoid the finger called the "amah" - unless excessive filth requires using all the fingers.

paragraphs: Women too must recite "Asher Yatzar," and should make an effort to learn it by heart, for it is very necessary and a great rectification is accomplished through it; it contains forty-five words corresponding to the numerical value of "Adam," and its secrets are many. Every person should understand the plain meaning of the wording of the blessing, so that he knows what he is saying.

clarification.explanation: Women too are obligated to recite "Asher Yatzar," and should make an effort to learn it by heart, for this blessing is very important and accomplishes a great spiritual rectification - it contains forty-five (45) words, corresponding to the numerical value of "Adam" [man], and it has many secrets. Every person should understand the plain meaning of the wording of the blessing, so as to know what he is saying.
takeaways: Women are obligated in the blessing "Asher Yatzar," and everyone - men and women alike - should learn it by heart and understand its plain meaning, due to its great spiritual importance.

paragraphs: It is forbidden to contemplate words of Torah in the bathroom, in soiled alleyways, and likewise in the inner chamber of the bathhouse; and the same law applies that it is forbidden to contemplate matters of mitzvah there, whether concerning charity, the needs of Shabbat, or the needs of sukkah, lulav, matzah, and the like. And one should be careful in the bathhouse not to mention the name of a person called "Shalom," or a person called "Abd-Allah" [servant of God], which is a name of Heaven in Arabic; and likewise one should not mention the word "Shabbat," for it is stated in the holy Zohar, "Shabbat is a name of the Holy One, blessed be He," and it is likewise called "Shalom."

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to contemplate words of Torah in the bathroom, in soiled alleyways, and likewise in the inner room of the bathhouse. Likewise it is forbidden to contemplate matters of mitzvah in these places as well - whether concerning charity, preparations for Shabbat, sukkah, lulav, matzah, and the like. One must be especially careful in the bathhouse not to mention the name of a person called "Shalom" or a person called "Abd-Allah" (which is actually a name of Heaven in Arabic), and likewise not to mention the word "Shabbat," for it is written in the holy Zohar that "Shabbat is a name of the Holy One, blessed be He" - Shabbat itself is called by the name "Shalom," and therefore both of these names are considered holy names that may not be mentioned in unclean places.
takeaways: It is forbidden to contemplate words of Torah or matters of mitzvah in the bathroom, in soiled alleyways, or in the inner chamber of the bathhouse.
In the bathhouse one must also be careful not to mention names hinting at holiness - such as "Shalom," "Abd-Allah," or "Shabbat" (since Shabbat itself is also called "Shalom").
